title: Septoplasty
subtitle: Stay under the perichondrium, leave the L-strut

sources.org: American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Foundation (AAO-HNSF)
sources.title: Clinical consensus statement: septoplasty with or without inferior turbinate reduction (Han JK et al., Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg)

indications: Nasal obstruction attributable to a septal deviation on examination, persisting after an adequate trial of medical treatment for any coexisting rhinitis, usually a topical nasal steroid.
Access for other endonasal surgery, such as endoscopic sinus surgery, dacryocystorhinostomy or endoscopic skull base surgery, when the deviation blocks the route.
Recurrent epistaxis from a septal spur that cannot be controlled otherwise, or a spur that prevents access to the bleeding point.
Harvest of septal cartilage as a graft for other reconstruction.
contraindications: Obstruction that is mainly from rhinitis, polyps or turbinate hypertrophy rather than the septum. Treat the real cause.
Uncorrected bleeding disorder or anticoagulation that cannot be safely interrupted.
Active cocaine use or granulomatous disease (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, sarcoidosis) involving the septum, which predispose to perforation. Consider a septal biopsy and serology instead.
An external nasal deformity that the patient expects to be corrected. A septoplasty does not change the shape of the nose; that is a septorhinoplasty conversation.
preparation: Examine with a nasendoscope and record which side and level are obstructed: caudal, high dorsal, or posterior bony septum and spur. A caudal deviation changes the incision.
Document the baseline external nose with photographs or a clear note, since patients notice and attribute any later change in shape to the operation.
Ask about smoking, cocaine and intranasal drug use, previous nasal surgery and nasal trauma.

Consent risks to discuss: bleeding and the possible need for packing, septal haematoma and abscess, septal perforation, persistent or recurrent obstruction and revision surgery, change in nasal shape including saddling or tip drop, numbness of the upper front teeth, adhesions, reduced sense of smell, and rarely cerebrospinal fluid leak.
Stop antiplatelets and anticoagulants according to local perioperative guidance and in agreement with the prescriber.
positioning: Supine with a head ring, head slightly flexed on the neck and turned a little towards the surgeon, with 15 to 20 degrees of head-up tilt.
Reinforced or preformed oral tube fixed in the midline of the lower lip, away from the field, and a throat pack if agreed.
Eyes taped and protected: the instruments work centimetres from the medial orbit.
equipment: Headlight, nasal specula of several lengths (including a Killian or Cottle long-bladed speculum), and a zero degree endoscope for endoscopic septoplasty.
Cottle and Freer elevators, scalpel with a 15 blade, Ballenger swivel knife, Luc or Takahashi forceps, through-cutting (Jansen-Middleton) forceps, chisel or osteotome and mallet.
Topical vasoconstrictor (for example xylometazoline, oxymetazoline, or cocaine-based solutions where local policy allows, within dose limits), and local anaesthetic with adrenaline for infiltration.
Absorbable quilting suture on a straight or small curved needle, silicone splints, and nasal packs if the surgeon chooses to use them.
anatomy: The septum is the quadrilateral cartilage in front, the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid above and behind, and the vomer below and behind, sitting on the maxillary crest and nasal crest of the palatine bone.

The cartilage is covered by mucoperichondrium and the bone by mucoperiosteum. The plane deep to the perichondrium is nearly avascular and is the plane of the operation; above it the mucosa bleeds and tears.

Dorsal and caudal support of the nasal tip and bridge comes from an L-shaped strut of cartilage. A commonly taught minimum is 1 cm of dorsal and caudal strut; loss of it causes a saddle nose or tip drop.
The perpendicular plate is continuous with the cribriform plate. Twisting it rather than cutting it can fracture the skull base and cause a cerebrospinal fluid leak.
The nasopalatine nerve and vessels run along the septum to the incisive canal; disrupting them at the anterior maxillary crest causes numbness of the upper incisors.
criticalSafety: The plane is under the perichondrium. Mucosa that is pink and bleeding means you are above it; cartilage that looks blue-white and smooth means you are in it.
Preserve the dorsal and caudal L-strut. Resect what is deviated, not what is reachable.
Cut the bony septum with through-cutting instruments. Never twist or rock the perpendicular plate.
Tears in both flaps at the same level are the cause of perforations. If they occur, repair at least one side and replace cartilage between them.
structuresAtRisk: Dorsal and caudal L-strut (saddle nose, tip drop)
Cribriform plate and skull base (cerebrospinal fluid leak)
Orbit and nasolacrimal system with posterior or high dissection
commonErrors: Elevating in a submucosal rather than subperichondrial plane, which bleeds and tears.
Leaving a posterior bony spur or a high deviation untreated, so the obstruction persists.
Resecting too much dorsal or caudal cartilage while chasing a deviation that should have been scored, repositioned or left.
Ignoring a caudal deviation, which needs a hemitransfixion approach and repositioning on the nasal spine rather than a Killian incision.
complications: Bleeding, early or delayed, sometimes needing packing or return to theatre.
Septal haematoma, which can become a septal abscess and destroy cartilage, causing a saddle nose. It presents as increasing obstruction and pain after an initially clear nose.
Septal perforation, often with crusting, whistling or bleeding.
Persistent obstruction, adhesions, change in nasal shape, numb upper incisors, reduced smell, cerebrospinal fluid leak, and toxic shock syndrome with retained packs.
postop: Remove packs, if used, according to the unit's protocol, usually the next morning. Splints are removed in clinic after about a week.
Saline nasal douching, no nose blowing for the first week or so, and sneeze with the mouth open.
Warn the patient that rising pain and worsening obstruction after the first day suggest a septal haematoma and need same-day review.
Routine antibiotics are not required for an uncomplicated septoplasty; follow local policy if packs are left in.

steps.emphasis: Confirm the patient understands that the shape of the nose is not being changed, and that obstruction from rhinitis will persist.
Nasendoscopy findings showing the deviation that matches the symptomatic side and level, and the record of a medical trial for rhinitis.
Antibiotic prophylaxis is not routine for septoplasty; follow local policy. Thromboprophylaxis by risk assessment.
Reinforced oral tube in the midline. A throat pack is recorded on the whiteboard because blood runs back into the pharynx throughout.
Head-up tilt of 15 to 20 degrees, eyes taped and protected, tube fixed away from the nose.
Aqueous antiseptic only around the eyes and face. Leave the nose and medial canthi in view.
Topical vasoconstrictor on patties first, then infiltrate under the mucoperichondrium on both sides of the septum until the mucosa blanches and lifts.
Inspect both flaps and the incision with the endoscope after the patties are removed and the blood pressure is normal.
Patties, packs and the throat pack counted out. A retained nasal patty is a retained swab.
State whether packs or splints are in and how the patient is to breathe; tell recovery that mouth breathing is expected and nasal bleeding through the packs is not.

step.septo.incision.title: Incision: Killian or hemitransfixion
step.septo.incision.why: The incision decides which part of the septum you can correct. A Killian incision protects the caudal strut; a hemitransfixion incision is needed when the caudal septum itself is deviated.
how: For a mid or posterior deviation, make a Killian incision through mucosa and perichondrium about 1 cm behind the caudal border of the septum, on the side chosen by the surgeon's handedness and the deviation.
For a caudal deviation or a dislocated caudal border, make a hemitransfixion incision at the caudal edge of the septal cartilage.
Cut through perichondrium on to the cartilage; scratch gently until the blue-white cartilage surface is seen before elevating.
pitfalls: A Killian incision placed too far forward that weakens the caudal strut.
Incising only mucosa, so the elevation starts in the wrong plane.

step.septo.flap.title: Raise the subperichondrial flap
step.septo.flap.why: The subperichondrial plane is avascular and strong. In it the flap survives and the septum heals; above it the flap is thin, bleeds and tears, and tears become perforations.
how: Lift the perichondrium off the cartilage with the sharp end of a Cottle or Freer elevator, sweeping backwards and upwards with the instrument kept against the cartilage.
Extend the elevation over the whole deviated area and down to the floor of the nose, keeping it in one sheet.
Work slowly over a convexity or old fracture line, where the flap is thinnest and adherent. Use the endoscope if the view is poor.
Keep the suction tip against the cartilage, not the flap.
pitfalls: Elevating pink, bleeding tissue: you are submucosal; go back and re-find the cartilage.
Tearing the flap over a sharp spur by forcing the elevator across it rather than around it.

step.septo.bony-junction.title: Cross to the opposite side at the bony-cartilaginous junction
step.septo.bony-junction.why: Most deviations involve both cartilage and bone. Freeing the cartilage from the bone posteriorly and raising the contralateral flap gives access to both without detaching the strut.
how: Separate the quadrilateral cartilage from the perpendicular plate and vomer with the blunt end of the elevator along the chondro-osseous junction.
Raise the subperiosteal flap on the opposite side of the bony septum, keeping the opposite cartilage flap attached where it is not needed.
Where the cartilage is deviated off the maxillary crest inferiorly, release it from the crest so it can swing back to the midline.
pitfalls: Disarticulating the cartilage from the bone along its full height, including high dorsally, which destabilises the dorsum.
Tearing the opposite flap at exactly the level of an existing tear on the first side.

step.septo.resection.title: Resect deviated cartilage and bone, preserve the L-strut
step.septo.resection.why: Only the deviated segment needs to go. The dorsal and caudal strut holds up the bridge and the tip, and the cribriform plate sits on top of the perpendicular plate, so what you remove and how you remove it both matter.
how: Mark the dorsal and caudal strut you will leave, commonly at least 1 cm each, and resect deviated cartilage behind and below it with the swivel knife or scalpel.
Remove deviated perpendicular plate and vomer with through-cutting forceps. Cut it free before removing it; never twist or rock bone attached to the skull base.
Keep straight pieces of resected cartilage. Crushed or straightened cartilage can be replaced between the flaps at the end to support them.
Check with the speculum and endoscope that the airway on both sides is now open along its whole length.
pitfalls: Resecting a high dorsal deviation in the strut, which causes a saddle deformity. Scoring, splinting or a referral for septorhinoplasty is safer.
Twisting the perpendicular plate: a clear fluid leak afterwards is cerebrospinal fluid until proven otherwise.

step.septo.maxillary-crest.title: Deal with the maxillary crest and spur
step.septo.maxillary-crest.why: A basal spur or a cartilage edge dislocated off the maxillary crest is the commonest cause of persisting obstruction, and the commonest site of a flap tear.
how: Raise the inferior tunnel along the floor of the nose separately and join it to the upper tunnel at the spur, so the flap is lifted around the spur from both directions.
Reduce the spur with a chisel or gouge, or remove it with forceps, keeping the flap protected with the speculum blade.
Avoid deep chiselling at the front of the crest near the incisive canal.
pitfalls: Chiselling the spur with the flap still stretched over it.
Leaving a spur behind because it was not visible through the speculum; check with the endoscope.

step.septo.tear-bailout.title: Bail-out: opposing flap tears or loss of support
step.septo.tear-bailout.why: A tear on one side heals. Tears on both sides at the same level, with no cartilage between them, become a permanent perforation. A destabilised strut becomes a deformity. Both are rescued in theatre, not in clinic.
how: If both flaps are torn at the same level, close at least one side with a fine absorbable suture and place a piece of straightened cartilage or crushed cartilage between the flaps.
If the caudal strut has been dislocated or weakened, fix it back to the nasal spine or splint it, and tell the consultant before closing.
If clear fluid is seen from high in the nose, stop, examine the skull base endoscopically and call a senior. A recognised leak is repaired at the time where possible.
pitfalls: Leaving opposing tears unrepaired because the operation is otherwise finished.
Not recording a tear or a leak in the operative note, so the follow-up clinic does not look for the consequence.

step.septo.close-quilt.title: Close the incision, quilt the flaps, splint
step.septo.close-quilt.why: The space between the flaps fills with blood if it is left open. Quilting sutures or splints obliterate the dead space and prevent a septal haematoma, often without the discomfort of packs.
how: Close the incision with interrupted absorbable sutures.
Place a running transseptal quilting suture from front to back to hold both flaps against the remaining septum.
Insert silicone splints on both sides and secure them with a transseptal suture, or use packs according to surgeon preference.
Look along each side with the endoscope to confirm the airway is open and nothing is bleeding.
pitfalls: Quilting sutures pulled tight enough to strangulate the flap.
Splints left without a documented removal date.
